passage:
Monday: Pallavi handed out flyers about the dry lake behind her school. Uday grinned. "Nobody reads those. Does a flyer refill a lake?" Her ears burned, but she only said, "The town office measured the water level last year. I'll bring the numbers."
Thursday: She showed him a printed report and a list of three lakes that were cleaned after local petitions. "It took four years," she admitted. "So yes, it's slow." Uday shrugged. "Slow and pointless are close cousins."
Two Saturdays later: Pallavi was at the lake edge with the cleanup group, pulling plastic from the bank. Uday arrived late, holding a garbage bag. "Just this once," he said. She handed him gloves and didn't gloat.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say she would bring after Uday mocked the flyers?
qa.a: She said she would bring the numbers, since the town office measured the water level last year.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Uday mocked the flyers, and how does the scene show it?
qa.a: Her ears burned, which suggests hurt or anger, yet she answered with a fact and an offer to bring numbers instead of snapping back.

qa.q: What could Pallavi try if Uday keeps calling her cause pointless?
qa.a: She could keep answering with facts and patience, admit that change is slow, and put her effort into the Saturday cleanups where she can see a real difference.

qa.q: Why might Uday have turned up with a garbage bag after mocking her work?
qa.a: The report may have made him curious, and he seems a little awkward about it, since he arrives late and says "Just this once".

grounding: Shows a teen answering peers' scorn with facts, accepting slow change and acting locally.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 10C, end of term

Ramesh has run the waste-segregation drive in our block since August. Every morning he checks the three bins and puts up a chart. It has not been easy for him.

On Monday, in front of the class, Anand said, "What's the point? The garbage truck mixes it all anyway. You're wasting everyone's time." A few boys laughed. I saw Ramesh's jaw tighten.

He waited a moment. Then he said, "The truck used to mix it. Since October the municipality sends a separate van for dry waste. Our block sent two hundred kilos to recycling last month. It's small. But it's real." Anand shrugged. "Still won't save the planet." Ramesh said, "No. It'll make our block cleaner, though."

Afterwards he told me he felt like giving up. We talked about how change is slow and that he had chosen a place where he could make a real difference. He decided to keep going and to invite Anand to help weigh the bags next week. Anand, to my surprise, said yes.

qa.q: How many kilos did the block send to recycling last month?
qa.a: The block sent two hundred kilos to recycling last month.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's tightening jaw suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ramesh felt hurt and angry when Anand called the drive pointless in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do well when Anand challenged him?
qa.a: Ramesh answered with calm facts about the separate van and the recycling total, and admitted the change was small but real.

qa.q: Why might Anand have agreed to help weigh the bags?
qa.a: Anand may have been more curious than he let on, and Ramesh's patient answer made the invitation feel sincere, not like a trap.

grounding: It shows a teen whose activism is called pointless by peers, answering with facts and patience, accepting that change is slow and acting where he can make a difference.

passage:
Thursday

Kishore said it again at lunch. "Afreen, your ramp campaign is useless. The management will never build it. Why bother?"

I wanted to throw my water bottle at him. Instead I counted to five and said, "Okay, here's why." I told him about Raghu in 8B, who uses a wheelchair and has to be carried up the six steps to the library every day by two peons. I told him the building rules say new schools must have ramps, and old ones are supposed to add them.

He said, "Rules mean nothing here."

I said, "Maybe. But the principal agreed to meet our group next Tuesday. That's more than nothing."

He didn't answer.

I know it might take a year. Maybe more. I'm trying to accept that. But I'm not trying to fix the whole country. I'm trying to fix six steps.

Raghu said thank you today, just for trying. That's enough for this week.

Afreen

qa.q: How many steps lead up to the library?
qa.a: Six steps lead up to the library.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when Kishore called the campaign useless?
qa.a: Afreen felt angry and frustrated enough to want to throw a water bottle at him.

qa.q: Why is Afreen's focus on six steps a wise choice?
qa.a: It picks a real change Afreen can influence, which keeps the campaign going even though larger change is slow.

qa.q: How might Raghu feel about the campaign?
qa.a: Raghu seems grateful and touched, since he thanked Afreen just for trying, even before any ramp is built.

grounding: It shows a teen whose activism is challenged by a peer as pointless, answering with facts and patience, accepting slow change and acting where a real difference is possible.
